newsitem.title: FRANCE: French pension bill debate runs into Wednesday.
newsitem.headline: French pension bill debate runs into Wednesday.

text.p: France's National Assembly has reserved time on Wednesday morning to continue the second reading of a bill to introduce pension funds in France.

A vote was originally expected late on Tuesday but the reservation of extra time on Wednesday, amid a vow by opposition parties to create procedural obstacles before a vote, meant the vote looked certain to be delayed until Wednesday.

The bill has sparked strong opposition from trade unions who say it could drain as much as six billion francs from the basic social security retirement benefits system and another 12 billion from the ARRCO and AGIRC obligatory top-up regimes.

They say employers will be tempted to offer contributions to private pension schemes instead of pay rises, because pay rises would not qualify for exemption from payment of social security charges, which fund pensions, sickness and welfare benefits.
The opposition Socialists and Communists have also objected.

But Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said on Tuesday there was no question of compromising on the controversial clause in the bill which exempts employers from paying social security charges on money they contribute to private pensions on behalf of staff.
The bill's author, Jean-Pierre Thomas, told the National Assembly on Tuesday the impact would be far less than unions claimed.

Using the hypothesis of a 10 percent rise in salaries versus the alternative of private pension contributions worth the equivalent amount, the social security contributions that would be foregone in choosing the second option would only come to 2.1 billion francs, he said.

That comprised 900 million francs foregone in social security contributions, and 600 million each for the ARRCO and AGIRC obligatory top-up regimes which are the second mainstay of the current pay-as-you-go, state-backed pension system.
Once the bill goes through the National Assembly, or lower house, it must return to the Senate for a second reading.
